implementation_notes: Python cannot truly prevent mutation - PEP 557 says so explicitly - so the idiom is the strongest available approximation: @dataclass(frozen=True) replaces __setattr__ and __delattr__ and raises FrozenInstanceError on assignment, adds __hash__ when eq=True, and dataclasses.replace() is the wither that returns a new instance. Frozen blocks rebinding only, so fields that must not change are declared as tuple, frozenset or types.MappingProxyType, and a proxy is a read-only view rather than a copy, so the underlying dict must stay private. The classic hand-written class (private attributes, properties, copy-with methods) is still justified where the generated __init__ is too permissive, where a custom construction API is part of the type, or on versions before dataclasses (3.7).
code_sketch:
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Config:
    name: str
    ports: tuple[int, ...] = ()

base = Config("api", (8080,))
next_cfg = replace(base, ports=base.ports + (8443,))   # new value; base unchanged
# dict-shaped state: types.MappingProxyType over a private dict; sets: frozenset
pitfalls: Frozen blocks attribute rebinding only: a field holding a list, dict or set stays mutable, so a frozen dataclass with mutable fields is only shallowly immutable.
types.MappingProxyType is a live read-only view: whoever holds the original dict can still change it and every holder of the proxy sees the change.
Hashability depends on the fields: a frozen dataclass containing a list still raises TypeError when hashed, and the failure appears only when the value is used as a key.
dataclasses.replace() calls __init__ and __post_init__ again and copies shallowly, so validation re-runs and nested mutable objects are shared with the original.
